caption:
Departing flights were stopped at airports across the US on Friday after a communications failure hit air traffic control centers.
It came three days after the FAA said its AI route planning tool, SMART, was expanding to all 22 centers.
DHS is checking for a link. The company behind SMART says there is none, and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blames an old, overloaded system.

Should AI be anywhere near air traffic control?

Follow @neurafeed.ai for daily AI news.

Source: KXAN · Photo: AP Photo/Ryan Murphy

site_article.summary: A communications failure led the FAA to stop departing flights at airports across the United States on November 13, 2026. site_article.seo_title: FAA ground stop: officials examine SMART AI air traffic tool
site_article.seo_description: A nationwide FAA ground stop on November 13, 2026 followed a communications failure. DHS is checking whether the new SMART AI tool played a role.
site_article.answer_summary: No cause has been confirmed. The FAA reported a communications failure at air traffic control centers, DHS is checking whether the SMART AI tool was involved, and the company behind SMART says it was not.

paragraphs.text: The Federal Aviation Administration ordered a nationwide ground stop for departing flights on the afternoon of Friday, November 13, 2026, after a communications problem affected air traffic control operations, according to KXAN and Futurism. Airports including Austin-Bergstrom International confirmed they were affected.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a post on X that the stop followed a communication issue affecting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers and that FAA technicians were investigating, Futurism reported. KRON4 noted that it was only the third nationwide ground stop, after the September 11, 2001 attacks and a key FAA computer malfunction in January 2023.

The timing has drawn attention to SMART, short for Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories. The FAA said on November 10 that the tool was expanding across the nation to all 22 air route traffic control centers, three days before the ground stop, according to KXAN. SMART first went into use in the airspace around Washington, D.C. in September.

KXAN described SMART as a cloud based platform that combines about 200 data streams, including airline schedules, flight paths, weather, airport capacity and controller staffing, and uses AI to predict traffic flows and recommend route and departure changes. The FAA says it is a planning tool, not an aircraft control system: it cannot take control of aircraft or replace controllers, and local facility leaders can accept or reject its suggestions. Futurism put the cost at just under $1 billion.
Earlier FAA figures cited by KRON4 said SMART had rerouted 180 flights, saving an average of 10 minutes and 80 gallons of fuel per flight.
What officials and the developer said

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said his department is working with other federal agencies, including through the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, to determine whether the new AI technology contributed to the disruption, News4JAX reported. He described the event as a telecommunications issue and said there was no threat to the public. Officials have not established that the AI system caused the problem.
Air Space Intelligence, the contractor behind SMART, said in a statement on X that the ground stop was not based on or a result of the SMART system, according to Futurism.

Duffy, speaking at a White House briefing, pointed instead to aging infrastructure, saying an old system went down everywhere after it was overloaded, KXAN reported. He said he wanted $50 billion in emergency funding for upgrades, more than the roughly $30 billion the White House had requested earlier the same day.

More than 20 members of Congress wrote to the Government Accountability Office on October 13 asking for an independent review of how the FAA developed and rolled out SMART, according to KXAN. The lawmakers questioned whether frontline controllers had enough input and training, whether safety evaluations were adequate, and why the tool was first deployed in congested airspace such as the National Capital Region. They also raised the risk that AI could interfere with experienced controllers or produce inaccurate safety critical information.

The Department of Transportation is separately spending $12.5 billion on modernization projects such as telecommunications upgrades, new radios and radar, and electronic flight strips, with completion expected by the end of 2028, KXAN reported.

For now, the public record points in two directions. The government's own description of the failure centers on communications systems, and the transportation secretary blamed old equipment, while the AI tool's expansion happened days earlier and DHS has kept it on the list of possible factors. Without a published cause, the episode mainly shows how closely any new AI system in safety critical infrastructure will be examined when something goes wrong.
The next thing to watch is the FAA's account of what failed in its communications network, and whether the GAO review that lawmakers requested in October is expanded to cover the ground stop.
